question: What is the Naive Bayes assumption and how does it affect probability calculations?
answer: The Naive Bayes assumption, also known as the conditional independence assumption, states that the probabilities P(fi|c) are independent given the class c. This means that the presence or absence of a feature (word) in a document is not affected by the presence or absence of other features. As a result, these probabilities can be "naively" multiplied together to calculate the probability of all features given a class.  This assumption simplifies the calculation of probabilities and allows for the use of the formula P(f1, f2, ..., fn|c) = P(f1|c)·P(f2|c)·...·P(fn|c), which is used in the Naive Bayes classifier.

Perplexity is inversely proportional to the likelihood of the test sequence according to the model, so a lower perplexity indicates that a language model is a better predictor of the words in the test set.  In other words, if a language has a high branching factor (many possible next words), its perplexity will be higher, indicating that the language model is less accurate. Conversely, if a language has a low branching factor (fewer possible next words), its perplexity will be lower, indicating that the language model is more accurate.
